knownFailurePatterns: Cloudinary assets orphaned because the public_id was never persisted and had to be reverse-engineered from the delivery URL.
A delete loop that throws on the first failure, skipping the Firestore write and leaving records that can never be cleared.
cloudinary.uploader.destroy returning 'not found' treated as an error, making an already-deleted asset permanently unclearable.
destroy() called without resource_type, which defaults to 'image' and silently fails for raw and video assets.
API routes that mutate Cloudinary or Firestore without verifying the caller's Firebase ID token.
Firestore rules written as `request.auth != null || request.auth == null`, which is unconditionally true.
Firestore rules relying on `A && B || C` precedence, which grants access on C alone.
Server secrets stored in NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables, which Next.js inlines into the client bundle on any client-side reference.
Read-modify-write with getDoc followed by setDoc, which drops entries when concurrent upload callbacks race.

invariants.description: Secrets must not live in NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables
invariants.why: Next.js inlines every NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable into the client bundle as soon as anything client-side references it.

invariants.description: Upload and delete routes must verify the caller's ID token
invariants.why: These routes mutate Cloudinary and Firestore; unauthenticated access lets anyone destroy the account's assets.

invariants.description: Firestore rules must not contain always-true auth conditions
invariants.why: `request.auth != null || request.auth == null` is unconditionally true and exposes the collection to everyone.

invariants.description: Cloudinary destroy calls must pass resource_type
invariants.why: destroy() defaults to resource_type 'image', so raw and video assets are silently never deleted.
